claims.text: Machine-learning interatomic potentials combined with direct-coexistence or interface-pinning methods can accurately predict melting temperatures of high-melting refractory materials.
The proposed ML-based approach can predict entropy and enthalpy of fusion and volume change at melting.
The proposed approach is more cost-effective than ab initio molecular-dynamics thermodynamic integration.
The target material is a high-melting refractory material in a solid phase near its melting point.
ML interatomic potentials trained on DFT data can replace expensive ab initio molecular dynamics and thermodynamic integration for the proposed melting calculations.
Efficient free-energy schemes can be run using ML interatomic potentials.
Reliable melting simulations require sufficiently large simulation cells and sufficiently long simulation times.
DFT-level accuracy is required under the stated high-temperature conditions.
The ML interatomic potential captures local atomic interactions and the energetic landscapes of both solid and liquid phases.
Training on high-fidelity DFT data allows the ML potential to reproduce the refractory material's solid- and liquid-state energetics accurately.
Coupling the ML potential to direct coexistence or interface pinning enables efficient sampling of the relevant free-energy landscape.
Sampling that free-energy landscape enables determination of melting temperature, fusion entropy, fusion enthalpy, and volume change at melting.
The ML-based predictions are expected to deviate by less than 10% from full DFT-AIMD thermodynamic-integration results.
The ML-based method will substantially reduce computational cost relative to full DFT-AIMD thermodynamic integration.
The computational savings will enable high-throughput evaluations.
Traditional DFT-based melting calculations use computationally expensive thermodynamic integration via ab initio molecular dynamics.
The reliability of the approach is limited by the quality and transferability of the ML potential.
Extreme conditions or compositions absent from the training set can produce significant deviations from DFT results.
